live.name: NICKEL KIMBALL
live.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL: a threat actor tracked under many names
live.in_short: NICKEL KIMBALL is the Secureworks name for an actor also known as Kimsuky and APT43. The catalogue lists its aliases and tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL KIMBALL is the name Secureworks uses for this threat actor.
Other vendors track it under many other names, including APT43, Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, Velvet Chollima, THALLIUM, TA427 and Black Banshee.
The catalogue lists eight tools tied to the actor: BabyShark, FastFire, FastSpy, FireViewer, KONNI, KimJongRAT, Kimsuky and ReconShark.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL KIMBALL is the Secureworks name for an actor that others track under many names, including APT43, Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, Velvet Chollima, Springtail and THALLIUM.
The catalogue record lists tools tied to the actor, including BabyShark, ReconShark, KONNI and KimJongRAT.
Microsoft, as reported by BleepingComputer, describes Kimsuky (also called Emerald Sleet or Velvet Chollima) as a North Korean state actor.

Symantec calls Springtail (aka Kimsuky) a North Korean espionage group. It says the U.S. government has described the group as a unit of North Korea's military intelligence organization, the Reconnaissance General Bureau.
Sekoia and Kudelski Security say some DPRK experts regard Kimsuky as a mega-cluster with several branches, such as TA406 and TA408. They also note that vendors divide and name clusters differently.

Genians says some researchers class KONNI, Kimsuky and APT37 as one group, because their targets and infrastructure overlap. It cites an MSMT report that assesses Kimsuky and KONNI as distinct groups.
Microsoft says Kimsuky targeted people in international affairs organizations, NGOs, government agencies and media companies in limited attacks from January 2025.
Genians assesses, with moderate confidence, that Kimsuky ran a 2026 campaign against South Korean policy and security professionals.
South Korea's National Police Agency said Kimsuky, Lazarus and Andariel breached South Korean defense companies and their subcontractors to steal defense technology data.
Breakglass Intelligence reports Kimsuky phishing lures aimed at South Korean Naver users.
AhnLab reported signs of AppleSeed, which it says Kimsuky mainly uses, being spread to maintenance contractors of a military unit in July 2022.

Microsoft says Kimsuky adopted ClickFix-style tactics. A fake South Korean official contacts the target, sends a PDF, and tells them to run code in PowerShell as administrator. The code installs a browser-based remote desktop tool.

AhnLab says Kimsuky spreads the PebbleDash backdoor mainly through spear-phishing emails with shortcut files disguised as documents. The chain also patches a Windows system file to bypass remote desktop authentication.
Symantec describes Springtail's use of trojanized software installers. It also describes phishing in which the actor poses as journalists, academics and experts in East Asian affairs.
Breakglass Intelligence attributes, with high confidence, a three-stage chain to Kimsuky. It starts from a help file disguised as API documentation and ends in a keylogger with clipboard monitoring.

ENKI WhiteHat attributes new DOCSWAP Android malware to Kimsuky, citing shared infrastructure, a known phishing string and Korean-language comments. It describes this as strong evidence, not definitive confirmation.
S2W suspects the DocSwap Android app is linked to a North Korean-backed group, possibly connected to Kimsuky. The app logs keystrokes through accessibility services.

In January 2021, a report citing ESTsecurity said Thallium altered the installer of a private stock investment messaging app. The researchers said the motive was unclear, either money or spying on traders.

In December 2022, South Korean officials said hackers believed to be operating from North Korea breached the KAERI nuclear research body through a VPN flaw. One of thirteen IP addresses involved was linked to infrastructure used by Kimsuky.

According to South Korea's National Police Agency, Kimsuky exploited an email server flaw at a defense subcontractor between April and July 2023. The flaw allowed large files to be downloaded without authentication.
South Korea's NCSC says that in January 2024 Kimsuky compromised a construction trade website. It used the site to spread trojanized security installers signed with a valid certificate.
Symantec reported Linux.Gomir, a backdoor it says Springtail developed. It appears to be a Linux version of the GoBear backdoor, which was used in a campaign that delivered Troll Stealer.
Treat unexpected installers, shortcut files and requests to paste commands into a terminal as suspect, even when they seem to come from a known contact.
Check software downloads against the vendor's own site before running them.
